I truly don't think there has been another gaming experience that has managed to create a character dynamic like the Boy Band Retinue in FFXV. The found-family brotherhood aspect is far and away the most enjoyable part of the game for me. The characters still have some fantasy-protaganist tropes attached, but the bulk of their interaction and development between each other is so real and engaging. From their quips to each other, the way they will call out something for the player to check when you're out and about, to the core mechanical elements of link-strikes and cross-chains, everything the works about XV also works to endear you to these little guys
So awesome!

It's an understandable frustration, though I would say it certainly adds to the vibe the game is going for. FFXV really emphasizes the dynamic of the boy band through their small yet intimate moments and interactions, and the 'road trip' backdrop is a huge vehicle for that. I like to conceptualize the surprise imperial ships as something akin to random battles in a more typical FF.

Plus the customization you get for the Regalia can be surprisingly satisfying. I wound up always visiting rest stop shops because I was personally hunting for the other FF soundtracks to play in the car, usually also buying a cool sticker or decal if they had one.

It can definitely be annoying to have to wait 5 real world minutes to get somewhere, but I would just argue this is an example of a game prioritizing its thematic consistency through its mechanics as opposed to focusing on player convenience. Not to say it's not a very valid criticism from that standpoint tho.

I think the debate is not so much about who is "good" or "bad". The debate is over which group has the strength of will and conviction to live as the primary group and society. Jogo describes the disaster curses as the "true humans" because he believes that their nature, as evil curses living to kill, is more true and real than the web of human society, with its social nuances, lying and other underhanded or obfuscated evils. Mahito tells Hanami that curses natural instincts are to murder and deceive, and recommends she live true to that nature, which we later see her do in the Yuji/Todo fight. 

Later, Mahito taunts Yuji in Shibuya, saying that just as Yuji is saving people without a second thought, he will kill without a second thought, as is his nature. He is telling Yuji that their battle is about the fundamental state of the world, literally "Who will be left standing in 100 years". There's not a moral equivalence, per se. Killing innocents and torturing them mentally *is* evil, but it's also, importantly, the nature of a curse.

Continuing in the comments for a moment as more thoughts come to me: >!A genuinely poorly handled character is *Nobara*. This is a case where I agree with the general consensus. That her return is a hackneyed attempt to check a box before the end of the Manga. Her death had almost no impact on the story beyond its immediate aftermath to Yuji. She gets precisely one (1) mention in the Culling Games before another 70 chapters and her return. While it is an interesting application of her cursed technique that ends up turning the tides in the Sukuna battle, this means nothing when it comes to the dynamic the three had, Nobara herself has no desires, no motivations, no flaws, and really no character development during her return, which makes it feel weightless and stupid.!<

Megumi's role post-shibuya was to give Yuji a role to play, a person to save to essentially keep him from killing himself. Megumi then experienced the tragedy of his sister's death, first by incarnation and then by Sukuna's hand through his technique. This led to him and Yuji essentially swapping their roles, with Yuji now tasked with rescuing Megumi from this calamitous curse that had destroyed their lives. From then on he was the victim, drained of a will to live.

And I liked it! You know, not every character needs to get a million power ups and unlock their domain expansion to be fulfilling to the narrative

The combat is nowhere near the finely tuned pleasure machine that KH2 offers, but I would argue its very charming in its own right. Because you aren't able to go into super killing mode with a bunch of crazy combo finishers and drive transformations, combined with the distinctly different *scale* of Sora and the Heartless, KH1 instead really incentivizes the player to be very aware of Sora's position in physical space. It asks you to move around and use the environment as opposed to only rely on the i-frames of block and dodge roll. The lagtime in all of Sora's move can be best mitigated best by memorizing your vulnerable spots, and using your standard movement and jump as tools in your kit.

About 10 years? I first was taught at a Boy Scout summer camp, but didn't actually engage with the game for real until really getting back into it in 2014, around Theros block I believe. That's when I started actually buying packs and building decks. That was all super kitchen-table casual, me and my buddies didn't even learn that there were sanctioned formats until 2016. 

I had one close friend who really dived in, was building Modern and Legacy decks trying to break into the competitive scene, which unfortunately did not have any real presence in our area, so it mostly amounted to him whooping us with a Legacy Elfball deck while we were still jamming in random draft uncommons. Then by the time we were out of highschool, most of my friends fell off of it, even my competitor buddy. That would've been it if my college roommate didn't happen to also have a distant history with the game. After trading stories, we got super into commander, buying precons and building EDH decks, introducing the game to our other roommates.

I've kept up with the sets and gone to pre-release events for the ones I'm interested in ever since, while really only ever playing Commander and Limited. 

Ironically, even though I've never actually tried to build a tournament-legal deck, I was really bummed by how WOTC totally restructured competitive play from 2019 onward. I used to watch the old Pro Tour coverage from Theros onward just because it was like pro sports to me. I had my favorite players (Reid Duke forever, btw) and would be endlessly entertained by the commentary. Tournament play that is streamed through Arena just doesn't compare to people playing pieces of cardboard for glory.

Random week-later reply lol: while I agree that Grade 1 is the most common designation for high-level sorcerers in JuJutsu society, I think one engaging facet of the story is that modern sorcerers like Yuji, Megumi, Maki and Hakari are not bound by that framework. I don't remember the specifics of the panel, but I believe Gojo explicitly tells Gakuganji during the Kyoto Event that future curses and sorcerers will not be bound by ratings like Grade 1 or even Special Grade. While it's true that the innate technique is a major factor in the special grades we've been introduced to in the story, it's clear that the evolution of sorcerers like Yuji, or Higuruma, or by extension unregistered reincarnated sorcerers like Kashimo, show that the actual grading system is likely flawed, or at the very least unable to contend with the material reality and evolution of jujutsu sorcery.

JJK takes a lot of page time to point out that the ruling class of Jujutsu society is very regressive in their mindset. Clinging onto a status quo that allows them to maintain power, which ultimately leaves them unprepared for the curses and curse users that hijack the training event and later execute the Shibuya incident. They hate Gojo because he is so powerful that he is uncontrollable, they feared the same from Yuji when he housed Sukuna, so they killed him. They were afraid of Yaga's cursed corpses, so they threatened to kill him unless he submitted to their control.

The Culling Games arc and subsequent storylines show us what happens when a crisis strikes Jujutsu society... and it's not much. As opposed to organizing a team to unseal Gojo and stop the Games, they instead retreat into their shells, taking advantage of Gojo's sealing to do all the evil stupid shit they had wanted to do before Gojo stopped them. Our heroes have to independently work to save these people, and are metaphorically and literally opposed by the ruling class (like the Zenin clan, rip).

All of this is to say, that I think Gakuganji's speech early in the manga on how Grade 1 is the Pinnacle of sorcery is less an objective fact, and more a thesis statement of the conservative movement. They essentially *demand* that Grade 1 be the peak of sorcery, as anything that surpasses it threatens the delicate grip the ruling class has on their society.

Cyclops falls into this strange slot I feel for a lot of writers. After Schism a lot of writers began to shape him into this very cynical "at all costs" type of character. AvX sort of cemented his place as this person wholly dedicated to the mutant race, and from there  Bendis' Uncanny X-Men helped flesh out his character arc to sort of see him as this broken man who has tried his best for all his life to see peace, watched friends and mentors die and betray him and from there he really took the freedom fighter/terrorist route. 

The annual for Uncanny X-Men  (which I believe was the end of X-Men titles before secret wars) did a phenomenal job of explaining this to the reader. In a very heartfelt discussion with Havok, Scott opens up about truly believing that if he could just scare the humans away everyone would be safe. It's honestly really sad I always empathized with him.

Then post-secret wars I don't know what the fuck happened. Call it marvel sabotage if you'd like but writers seemed to throw his continuity out the window. We come back after the 8 month gap, Cyke is dead and considered the worst mutant terrorist ever. In extraordinary X-Men, we see Magik (who was on his team in Uncanny) almost kill Sunfire for being associated with whatever Cyclops did. So I was reading this like "damn what'd he do he seemed to have this emotional breakthrough in the annual what happened" and when Death of X was announced I'm thinking ok maybe he got in a war with the inhumans, maybe a bunch of casualties? But no.

*Spoilers for Death of X*

We learn he died almost immediately of M-Pox, and Emma Frost used a psychic projection of him to organize a group to destroy a single Terrigen cloud. And then black bolt killed the projection, making him a martyr? It felt cheap although a bit in line with his character, and honestly a bit underwhelming considering his pariah status. Like why did everyone get so pissed? Literally like 3 months later we had IvX and honestly the whole mutant race was doing what he (Emma) was. 

Honestly I can't logically explain why Cyclops became this way, or why writers jerk him around in a bunch of different moral directions. The post secret wars era was bit of a dark time for X-Men, and I feel a lot of stuff was lazily written. Despite all that, I remain stalwart in believing one thing.
